chief_complaint: explosive thunderclap headache worst of life, vomiting
hpi_details: 55-year-old female is rushed to the ED by ambulance after suddenly collapsing to the floor grasping her head, screaming about the 'worst headache of my entire life' that peaked in intensity within seconds. Accompanied by severe nausea, profuse vomiting, and neck stiffness.
ideas: She thinks an intense migraine or severe pinched nerve in her neck caused a blood vessel in her head to burst.
concerns: She is terrified that she is suffering an aneurysm rupture or massive stroke that will cause sudden brain damage and kill her.
expectations: She hopes for immediate strong intravenous pain medication and an emergency brain scan to find out what happened inside her head.

investigation_events.title: STAT noncontrast CT of the head
investigation_events.availability_message: The STAT noncontrast head CT report is now available.

results.value: Acute subarachnoid blood throughout the basal cisterns and bilateral sylvian fissures, greatest in the anterior interhemispheric fissure; no midline shift

investigation_events.title: CT angiography of the cerebral arteries
investigation_events.availability_message: The cerebral CT angiography report is now available.

results.value: 7 mm irregular anterior communicating artery aneurysm, consistent with the source of the subarachnoid hemorrhage

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Subarachnoid Hemorrhage is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes a STAT noncontrast head CT, with lumbar puncture if the CT is negative but suspicion remains, for Subarachnoid Hemorrhage, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: explosive thunderclap headache worst of life, vomiting

Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Subarachnoid Hemorrhage SAH.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Migraine without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Thunderclap onset.
management_principles: Plan for Subarachnoid Hemorrhage SAH: STAT head CT, check lumbar puncture if CT negative
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 55F presenting with acute onset of a thunderclap headache, nausea, and vomiting.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 180/100, HR 105. Patient is lethargic but arousable, clutching her head in agony. Positive nuchal rigidity (meningismus). No focal motor deficits.
reference_soap.assessment: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH), highly suspicious for ruptured berry aneurysm.
reference_soap.plan: EMERGENCY. Obtain STAT noncontrast head CT; if negative but suspicion remains, pursue further evaluation with the appropriate pathway. Use IV antihypertensive therapy when needed to manage blood pressure, and give enteral nimodipine after aneurysmal SAH is confirmed to reduce delayed cerebral ischemia. Consult neurosurgery immediately for vascular imaging and aneurysm treatment.

teaching.one_liner: A ruptured aneurysm causing a sudden 'worst headache of life' reaching peak intensity within seconds.

must_ask.say: Did the headache reach its worst within seconds?
Is this the worst headache of your life?

history.answer: I had this sudden, explosive headache hit me out of nowhere about an hour ago, and I started throwing up violently. It's the worst pain I've ever felt in my entire life.
It struck completely out of the blue and went from nothing to a ten out of ten within literally a couple of seconds. It felt like an explosion inside my skull.
It started about an hour ago, and it has stayed at maximum intensity without letting up. I have never had a headache like this before.
It is all over my head, but it feels particularly intense in the back of my head and down into my neck.
It feels like my head is tearing apart or exploding. On a scale of one to ten, it is easily a ten.
Any slight movement, bending my neck, or opening my eyes makes the pain unbearable. Nothing has made it even a little bit better.
No, there were no flashing lights, blind spots, or tingling beforehand. It just slammed into me all at once.
Yes, I became intensely nauseated immediately after it started and threw up three times in the ambulance.
Yes, the emergency room lights and even normal talking hurt my head so much that I need to keep my eyes squeezed shut.
No, I don't have any eye watering, redness, runny nose, or drooping eyelids.
I haven't felt feverish or noticed any rash, but my neck feels completely stiff and locked up. Moving my chin down hurts terribly.
No, my arms and legs still feel strong, and I haven't noticed any numbness or slurred speech.
I collapsed to my knees from the shock of the pain, but I don't think I completely passed out, and I didn't have any shaking or seizures.
My vision is a bit blurry because of the sheer pain and keeping my eyes closed, but I'm not seeing double and my actual eyeballs don't hurt.
No, my temples are not tender to the touch, and I haven't had any pain when chewing or stiffness in my shoulders or hips.
No, I did not hit my head or have any kind of fall or accident before this started.
The paramedics gave me some IV fluids and nausea medicine, but I haven't taken any pills because it happened so fast and I couldn't keep anything down.
I was just doing routine chores around the house when it happened. I wasn't lifting anything heavy, coughing, or exercising.
history.topic: Possible triggers or activities at onset

history.answer: I've never been told I have high blood pressure, and I don't take any blood thinners or aspirin.
history.topic: High blood pressure and blood thinners

history.answer: No, nobody else at home has a headache, and our gas heating is off right now.
No, I don't have any history of cancer, and I am not immunocompromised.
It felt like a bomb went off inside my skull, and I thought an awful migraine or a burst blood vessel hit me out of nowhere.
I'm terrified that a blood vessel burst in my brain and I'm going to suffer permanent brain damage or die right here.
I need you to give me something strong through an IV for this agony and scan my head immediately.
I've been very healthy my entire life, with no chronic medical conditions.
I had an uncomplicated appendectomy twenty years ago, but no other surgeries or hospital stays.
I don't take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or vitamins.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only drink a glass of wine on special occasions, maybe once or twice a month, and had nothing today.
I work as an office administrator and live with my husband and adult daughter.
My father passed away from a heart attack in his seventies, and my mother is eighty and healthy. No one in my family had brain aneurysms that I know of.
I went through menopause two years ago, so my periods stopped completely back then.

exam.finding: Lethargic but arousable, clutching head in severe agony and distress, keeping eyes closed against the room light.
Blood pressure 180/100 mmHg, pulse 105 beats/min and regular, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Alert to person and place, but drowsy, slow to respond, and repeatedly groaning in pain.
Marked resistance to passive neck flexion with severe pain; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are both positive.
Pupils equal, round, and briskly reactive to light; extraocular movements intact without nystagmus; fundoscopic exam shows sharp optic disc margins without papilledema or retinal hemorrhage.
Cranial nerves II through XII grossly intact, with symmetric facial movements, no ptosis, and normal palate elevation.
Normal muscle tone; motor strength is 5/5 in both upper and lower extremities symmetrically without pronator drift.
Intact sensation to light touch throughout all dermatomes bilaterally.
Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric at the biceps, patellar, and Achilles tendons; plantar responses are flexor bilaterally.
No tenderness over the temporal arteries or frontal and maxillary sinuses.
